blocks.text: Sometimes a correct DP is still too slow or uses too much memory. DP optimization techniques are the tools that take a working solution and make it fit within the time and space limits.
These techniques do not change what the DP computes. They change how efficiently it computes it, by cutting away work or memory that is not truly needed.

blocks.caption: The main families of DP optimization
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406554121-495509289.png
A DP that is correct but exceeds the limits still fails. Interviews and contests set bounds precisely to force these optimizations, so recognising when and how to apply them is a real skill.
The two things we usually fight are space, when the table is too large to store, and time, when the transition is too expensive to repeat for every state.

items: Correctness is not enough if you blow the memory limit
Correctness is not enough if you blow the time limit
Optimizations keep the same answer while spending fewer resources

blocks.text: The most common optimization. If dp[i] only ever depends on dp[i minus 1], you do not need the whole 2D table, only the previous row. This drops space from O(n times m) to O(m).

blocks.caption: When each row only needs the row above, collapse the table into one rolling array
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406554121-908588403.png
Here is unique-paths on a grid, reduced to a single rolling row.

Rule of thumb:

If your transition reaches back only a fixed number of rows, you can keep just those rows. Two rows, one row, or even a few variables are often enough.
Sometimes the state count is fine but each transition scans a whole range, making the DP slow. The fix is to compute that range cheaply instead of looping over it every time.
Prefix Sums
If a transition needs the sum over a range of previous states, precompute prefix sums so each range total is a single subtraction rather than a loop.
Monotonic Deque
If a transition needs the minimum or maximum over a sliding window of previous states, a monotonic deque gives that in amortised constant time, turning an O(n squared) DP into O(n).
Binary Search
When a transition looks for a boundary in a sorted structure, binary search replaces a linear scan, as we saw in the fast Longest Increasing Subsequence.
For harder problems there are named techniques that reshape the transition itself. You do not need them often, but knowing they exist tells you when a problem expects one.

items: Divide and Conquer Optimization: when the best split point is monotonic, it cuts an O(n squared) layer to O(n log n).
Knuth Optimization: a similar idea for interval DP that brings O(n cubed) down to O(n squared).
Convex Hull Trick: when transitions are linear functions, it evaluates the best line quickly.

blocks.text: These are advanced and rarely required for standard interviews, but they are worth recognising by name so you know what a very tight constraint is hinting at.
When your DP is correct but too slow or too heavy, work through these questions.

items: Space too high? Check how many previous rows the transition truly needs, then keep only those.
Transition scans a range sum? Add prefix sums.
Transition scans a sliding window min or max? Use a monotonic deque.
Transition searches a sorted boundary? Use binary search.
Still too slow with a special structure? Consider divide and conquer, Knuth, or convex hull tricks.

blocks.text: Always get a correct DP working first, then optimize. It is far easier to speed up a solution you trust than to invent a fast one from nothing.
